description: We are students passionate about space, technology, and innovation. We aim to build an interactive Mars exploration platform using NASA data to help explorers plan routes, assess hazards, and discover scientific targets. We welcome members with skills in programming, UI/UX, data science, mapping, planetary science, research, or presentation
summary:
We built a Mars route planner that runs in your browser. We took NASA’s HiRISE data for the western edge of Jezero Crater and turned an 8 km area into a grid of small squares, 16 metres each, with a height for every square. From those heights, the app works out how steep the ground is everywhere and colours it green, yellow or red. You pick two points on the map, and it finds a route that avoids ground steeper than 15°. It then shows you the distance, the steepest part, an estimated risk level and an elevation graph.

The challenge was about bringing different Mars data together so explorers can plan a trip. We did that on one map. It matters because a bad step on Mars can end a mission. Our weather readings are just sample data for now, and the 15° limit is our own assumption
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

You open the website, see a 3D globe of Mars, and click on Jezero Crater to zoom into a 2D map. We prepared a small area of the crater (8 km wide) from NASA and USGS HiRISE data. It’s a grid of 16 m squares, and every square has a height. The app uses those heights to work out how steep the ground is and colours it green, yellow or red. You pick a start and an end point, and the app finds a route that avoids ground steeper than 15°. It then shows the distance, the steepest part, an estimated risk level and an elevation graph.

What benefits does it have?

It puts the photo, the terrain and the hazards on one map, so you can see why a route goes the way it does. It runs in a normal web browser with nothing to install, and a route comes back in a fraction of a second. It also tells you clearly when a point can’t be used, for example when it’s too steep or outside our area.

What is the intended impact?

We want to show how terrain data can turn into simple route planning for a Mars surface trip. It’s a prototype and a learning tool. It isn’t a real mission system, and we don’t claim it is.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

We used Python (rasterio, numpy, Pillow) to prepare the NASA data, and JavaScript to build the app. The website uses React and Vite, Leaflet for the 2D map and Three.js for the globe. We used USGS HiRISE terrain and image data, NASA Mars Trek and ArcGIS map tiles, Git and GitHub, VS Code and Vercel for hosting. We worked on normal laptops, and no special hardware was needed. We also used AI assistants to help plan and write parts of the code, and we tested the results ourselves.

How is it creative?

Our slope colours sit right on top of a real HiRISE photo of the same ground, so you can see steep ridges and craters under the colours. We also went from a whole-planet globe straight to a route planner in one flow. The routing runs in the browser itself, with no server needed.

What factors did our team consider?

We chose 16 m squares so the app stays fast, and we know that small rocks and steps disappear at that size. The terrain comes from satellite stereo images, so it has some error and can make slopes look steeper than they are. The 15° limit is our own assumption, taken from an example in the challenge guide. We call the result “estimated risk” and never “safe”, and our weather readings are labelled as sample data. We had only a couple of days, so we kept the design simple, and we gave each teammate a clear part: data, routing, map and interface.
